papers.title: TRPP Ion Channels Function in the π-Conformation Rather Than the α-Conformation
papers.abstract: PKD2 (TRPP1) is a TRPP ion channel whose dysfunction causes autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). Understanding its conformational states and gating mechanism is important for elucidating its function and for structure-based drug discovery. Cryo-EM structures of WT-PKD2 contain a local {pi}-helical turn in the S6 pore-lining helix ({pi}-conformation). In contrast, a fully -helical S6 (-conformation) was observed in the gain-of-function mutant F604P-PKD2 and interpreted as the open state, leading to the proposed {pi}-to- activation mechanism. However, whether the -conformation can support function has never been directly established. Here, using molecular dynamics simulations, we investigate the functional properties of the -and {pi}-conformations of PKD2. The -conformation remains dewetted unless the lower gate is widened beyond the conformational range observed in mammalian TRP channels. By contrast, the {pi}-conformation supports pore hydration and ion conduction following a small opening of the L677 gate, with simulated conductance comparable to experimental measurements. The closely related PKD2L1 (TRPP2) channel shows a similar dependence on conformation, with a hydrated {pi}-conformation and a dewetted -conformation. Together, these findings challenge the assignment of the -conformation as the conductive state and support a model in which the {pi}-conformation represents the functionally relevant state of TRPP channels. This model suggests that activation may involve an -to-{pi} transition rather than the previously proposed {pi}-to- transition, providing a new framework for understanding TRPP channel gating. This work sheds light on the molecular basis of polycystin channel dysfunction and could facilitate the development of PKD2-targeted therapeutic strategies for ADPKD.

papers.title: Growth-driven mechanical buckling as a mechanism of age-related tortuosity in human cerebral arteries
papers.abstract: Human cerebral arteries become increasingly, sometimes abnormally, winding with age, but the mechanical basis of this change remains incompletely understood. To examine how arterial bends form and what sets their spacing, we modeled a cerebral artery as a slender elastic vessel supported by surrounding tissue. The distance between its ends remains constant, and the vessel can bend only in a plane tangent to the brain surface. As its natural length increases, axial compression builds until the vessel buckles. Bending partly relieves the compression, and the resulting waves grow in amplitude as elongation continues. Arterial bending stiffness and tissue support determine the wavelength, which is much larger than and proportional to vessel diameter, with comparatively weak dependence on other parameters. Numerical simulations captured a pre-buckling phase, rapid amplification of waves, and slow post-buckling growth during continued elongation. We evaluated these predictions using three-dimensional centerlines of cerebral arteries reconstructed from magnetic resonance angiography in healthy adults. Older age was associated with greater arterial length and excess-length ratio. For arterial waves oriented mostly parallel to the brain surface, wavelength increased with vessel diameter. Both this relationship and the observed wavelength-to-diameter ratio were consistent with model predictions. However, wave amplitude was not significantly associated with age. Overall, the modeling and imaging results support growth-driven buckling and post-buckling deformation under spatial constraint as a plausible mechanical explanation for age-related cerebral arterial tortuosity. This framework links vascular aging to growth-driven instability and pattern formation, with potential applications to diseased arteries beyond the brain.

papers.title: Lipidic α-synuclein fibrils catalyze the formation of pathological mature fibrils
papers.abstract: The aggregation of -synuclein into amyloid fibrils is a hallmark of a collection of neurodegenerative diseases termed synucleinopathies, including Parkinson's disease (PD). Interactions between -synuclein and lipid membranes modulate -synuclein aggregation and can produce protofibril structures consisting of both protein and lipid, termed lipidic fibrils. These lipidic fibrils can mature into mature fibrils, which resemble ex vivo fibrils extracted from Lewy bodies found in post-mortem brain samples of PD patients. Here, through the combination of experiments and kinetic theory, we study the influence of lipids and lipidic fibrils on the formation of mature fibrils. We find that lipidic fibrils catalyze mature fibril formation via a heterogeneous primary nucleation mechanism, which lowers the activation energy barrier of mature fibril formation relative to lipid-independent primary nucleation. The final stage of the reaction is governed by mature fibril elongation becoming limited by the rate at which protein monomers dissociate from the metastable lipidic fibrils, confirming that fibrils form in order of stability following Ostwald's Rule of Stages. This mechanism is validated using the small molecule inhibitor ambroxol, which selectively suppresses the formation of lipidic fibrils and in this manner shifts the aggregation kinetics to the slow, lipid-independent pathway. Taken together, these findings reveal that lipidic fibrils act as on-pathway intermediates and accelerate the aggregation of mature fibrils, which could provide a quantitative framework to design novel therapeutic strategies to inhibit pathological -synuclein aggregation.

papers.title: The binding landscape of Ras/effector interactions provides insights on Ras switching and oncogenesis
papers.abstract: Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) regulate essential cellular processes, yet the evolutionary principles that shape their specificity, adaptability, and dysregulation in disease remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the evolution of a signaling PPI between the small GTPase Ras and its effector Nore1A, a tumor suppressor involved in Ras-mediated signaling. Ras acts as a molecular switch, engaging effectors in its GTP-bound active state and releasing them after GTP hydrolysis, whereas oncogenic mutations such as G12D lock Ras in the active state, promoting aberrant signaling in cancer. Using yeast surface display, deep mutational scanning, and data normalization, we systematically mapped the Ras/Nore1A binding landscape under different physiological and oncogenic states. We generated and screened $sim$33,000 Nore1A single and double mutants against RasWT and RasG12D in both GTP- and GDP-bound states. Our data revealed that most Nore1A mutations produce small-to-moderate decrease in Ras affinity, while a small number of substitutions enhance affinity. Unexpectedly, GTP hydrolysis causes minimal remodeling of the interaction landscape. Conversely, the oncogenic RasG12D mutation reshapes the binding landscape, revealing many Nore1A variants with enhanced and selective affinity for mutant Ras. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of Nore1A-Ras variant complexes suggest that the non-optimality of the Nore1A/RasG12D binding landscape arises, in part, from the greater intrinsic flexibility of RasG12D and the pronounced reduction in flexibility induced by affinity-enhancing Nore1A mutations. These findings demonstrate that disease-associated mutations can create new evolutionary trajectories in signaling PPIs by changing interaction dynamics and provide a framework for engineering selective protein-based inhibitors targeting oncogenic Ras variants.

papers.title: Evolution of Vesicle Shape Parameters Based on A Deep-Learning Based Image Analysis Framework Over Extended Time Periods
papers.abstract: A precise analysis of shape instabilities in cell-sized membrane compartments requires thorough quantification of the shape dynamics of individual components over extended periods. Herein, we have used phase-contrast microscopy to image giant unilamellar membrane vesicles (GUVs), which are widely used as model systems for cellular structures. GUVs were prepared in the fluid lamellar phase of 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine with and without cholesterol dissolved within a potato starch solution. The morphological changes and budding dynamics of individual GUVs with different chemical compositions were quantified using a deep-learning based image analysis framework over extended time periods, by using phase-contrast micrographs as input data. This automated framework integrates contour-based detection of the mother vesicle with precise segmentation of daughter compartments, thereby enabling explicit identification and tracking of mother and daughter vesicles at high temporal resolution. These findings further facilitate the measurement of the temporal evolution of vesicle morphometrics including area, and local membrane curvature during budding, that can be used as an input to develop computational models aimed at elucidating curvature-driven membrane remodeling in complex soft materials.

papers.title: Non-equilibrium cyclic conformations of DNA under electrokinetic confinement
papers.abstract: Classic nanofluidic devices harness geometric confinement to modulate single polymer conformation and control chain dynamics. While classic nanofluidic devices have given rise to a range of applications, they are fundamentally limited by the static nature of their construction, which restricts real time control over molecular conformations. The reversible electrokinetic confinement (RECON) technique enables time-dependent control of DNA conformations in nanowells via dynamic modulation of field-induced confinement. Here, we demonstrate that applying dynamically varying confinement using stochastic and periodic signals can drive the confined polymer to access a range of non-equilibrium states, with the distinct configurations quantified via their radius of gyration tensor. For periodic driving, the device allows controlled cycling across conformational states, with distinct hysteresis observed in the shape anisotropy modulation. We quantify the interplay between the driving frequency, driving amplitude, and resulting hysteresis. Overall, our results establish RECON as a platform for active manipulation of single molecules, opening new avenues for studying non-equilibrium polymer physics and developing high-throughput, dynamically tunable nanofluidic devices.

papers.title: A conserved thermodynamic signature links transcriptome organization to growth state
papers.abstract: Living systems operate far from thermodynamic equilibrium, sustaining complexity through continuous free-energy influx and heat dissipation. Yet the higher-order functional constraints imposed by non-equilibrium dynamics remain largely unexplored. To formalize how changes in cellular entropy production constrain intracellular organization across proliferative state transitions, we developed a stochastic-thermodynamic model linking reduced dissipative drive to transient increases in intracellular configurational entropy. Within this framework, we examined abundance-weighted predicted RNA folding stability as a transcriptome-level projection of the intracellular configurational remodelling. Consistent with the model, transcriptome reorganization across the cell cycle produces coordinated, phase-dependent changes in the distribution of transcript-level RNA folding free energies. Extending this analysis to stress adaptation, we find that human cancer cells exposed to molecularly targeted agents and nutrient-limited Escherichia coli converge on expressed RNA pools enriched for transcripts with less negative RNA folding free energies, despite marked heterogeneity in the transcriptional responses within each system. Opposing shifts during acquired resistance under continued drug exposure and bacterial recovery from starvation further support an association with growth state. Together, these findings suggest that transcriptome organization extends beyond gene-regulatory programs to collective biophysical properties that may reflect non-equilibrium constraints shaping cellular-state transitions.

papers.title: A Saliva-Inspired Model of Enzymatic Starch Hydrolysis by Alpha Amylase
papers.abstract: We demonstrate that the enzymatic activity of alpha-amylase (AA) can serve as an effective physicochemical trigger for membrane remodeling in giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs). This work provides insight into how primitive protocellular reactions directly translate into the membrane's mechanical responses. Analysis of the potato starch utilized in this work is composed of ~26% amylose and ~75% amylopectin. Quantitative DNS analysis revealed time- and concentration-dependent accumulation of reducing sugars during starch degradation by AA. The HPLC-RID chromatograms demonstrated the synthesis of glucose, maltose, maltotriose, maltotetraose, maltopentaose, maltohexaose, and maltoheptaose, with maltose and maltotriose as the major products. The accumulation of these soluble hydrolysis products gradually increases the osmolarity of the extracellular medium surrounding the vesicles, leading to osmotic asymmetry across the membrane. This biochemical framework provides a quantitative basis for understanding membrane deformation, curvature generation, vesicle deflation, and budding. In addition to the specific starch--$alpha$-amylase system studied here, our work uncovers a general mechanism by which external biochemical reactions control membrane shape transformations via osmotic coupling. Such enzyme-driven remodeling offers a simple yet powerful strategy for inducing dynamic structural changes in artificial cells. It may provide insight into primitive protocellular processes in which metabolic activity and membrane mechanics were inherently coupled.

papers.title: Electrostatic control of conformational dynamics drives proton translocation in respiratory Complex I
papers.abstract: Complex I is a large membrane protein that transduces redox energy into a proton motive force across a biological membrane, powering cellular respiration. Yet, despite significant experimental and computational efforts, its long-range proton translocation mechanism remains poorly understood. Here, we combine nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy and site-directed mutagenesis experiments with multiscale classical and hybrid quantum/classical (QM/MM) simulations to probe how conformational dynamics is linked to proton transfer reactions in the terminal antiporter module (Nqo12/NuoL/ND5) of Complex I. We show that protonation of a conserved proton-loading site (Lys329/His241Nqo12) in the terminal antiporter-like module gives rise to conformational changes that result in opening of the proton pathway. We further show that this protonation reaction is controlled by buried ion-pairs that modulate the barrier for proton translocation by intrinsic electric field effects. On a general level, our combined findings reveal how bioenergetic machines combine conformational dynamics with hydration transitions to establish efficient redox-driven proton pumps.

papers.title: Multispecies transport shapes electrochemical environments in perforated cells
papers.abstract: Cells maintain asymmetric electrochemical environments across selectively permeable plasma membranes. Ion channels on plasma membranes redistribute small ions, whereas large openings such as gasdermin pores allow both ions and proteins to cross the membrane, generating a multispecies transport regime. The transport of charged ions and proteins shapes electrochemical environments, leading to osmolarity changes, which in turn promotes water influx and cell swelling. Although biologists have observed the phenotypic progression from pore formation to cell swelling for decades, the molecular transport events underlying this progression remain elusive. To elucidate how pore formation drives downstream cellular effects, we establish quantitative multispecies transport frameworks to investigate gasdermin-perforated cells. We start by developing a reductionist model and benchmarking it against analytical Donnan predictions. We then explore three-dimensional geometries containing individual pores or pore clusters that form either simultaneously or sequentially. We reveal that ion-protein timescale separation generates non-canonical Donnan-like states, pore and cargo properties tune local transport, pore clustering modulates osmotic gradients, and sequential pore formation produces feedback-dependent dynamics. This work deepens our mechanistic understanding of cellular responses to membrane damage and informs the therapeutic design of pore-forming proteins with tunable cellular effects.

papers.title: Direct NMR evidence for transient binding of the vesicular SNARE protein synaptobrevin-2/VAMP2 to the α-synuclein C-terminus
papers.abstract: The protein -synuclein (-syn) plays a central role in several neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson's disease; however, its physiological function remains enigmatic. We provide direct evidence by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, microscale thermophoresis (MST), and biolayer interferometry (BLI) measurements that the -synuclein C-terminus binds to the vesicular SNARE (soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor) protein synaptobrevin-2 (syb-2), also known as VAMP2 (vesicle-associated membrane protein). The observed dissociation constant (Kd) in the 10 - 50 micromolar range falls within the estimated concentration range of -synuclein in neurons, while local concentrations may be substantially higher. NMR chemical shift perturbation (CSP) and paramagnetic relaxation enhancement (PRE) experiments mapped the binding site with residue-specific resolution to the -synuclein C-terminus (V118 - E137) and to the synaptobrevin-2 SNARE motif/linker domain interface (region A82 - K87), and also affected the synaptobrevin-2 N-terminus (M1 - S2). NMR CSPs and PREs indicate a transient interaction in the fast exchange (s-ms) regime. These transient weak binding interactions are characteristic of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and allow both proteins to engage in multiple binding interactions, thereby enabling -synuclein to play a regulatory role upstream of or during neuronal exocytosis. While the exact physiological role of -synuclein remains debated, the involvement of its pathological form in several neurodegenerative diseases (dubbed synucleinopathies) is well established. Our data suggest a direct link between proteins involved in neurodegeneration and neuronal exocytosis.

papers.title: Disulfide Crosslink Density is a Key Determinant in the Formation, Dynamics, and Maturation of Cysteine-rich Designer Biomolecular Condensates.
papers.abstract: Biomolecular condensates form through weak, multivalent, non-covalent interactions, but the role of covalent crosslinks in shaping their assembly and material properties remains poorly understood. We previously showed that disulfide bonds between cysteines in designer phase-separating peptides (PSPs) act as redox-reversible crosslinks that lower the saturation concentration (Csat) and help maintain condensate fluidity. Here, we ask which sequence features govern this behavior. We built two peptide libraries: one varying the inter-cysteine spacer length (2-10 residues) and one varying cysteine density (0-33%). Inter-cysteine spacers tuned condensate properties only modestly. Longer inter-cysteine lengths raised Csat from 300 to 900 M, showed greater fluidity (as assessed by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) recovery rate, and resisted loss of fluidity during maturation; all inter-cysteine length variants dissolved and reformed reversibly over three redox cycles. Cysteine density, in contrast, was the dominant control parameter. Increasing cysteine density lowered Csat about 60-fold (1.5 mM to 25 M) and reduced the fluidity by an order of magnitude. Its effect on fluidity was non-monotonic: condensates with up to ~14% cysteine density stayed liquid-like for 10 days, whereas those with 21-33% cysteine density in the peptide showed slower coalescence. Condensates with the highest densities also resisted dissolution under reducing conditions and showed sharply reduced uptake of a protein cargo (eGFP; ~60% to ~9%) and a small molecule (TMR, ~70% to ~45%), consistent with smaller mesh size. Together, these results identify disulfide crosslink density as a key lever for programming condensate assembly, viscoelasticity, redox responsiveness, and porosity. The results offer key design principles both for understanding cysteine-rich disordered proteins in biomolecular condensates and for engineering redox-responsive biomaterials.

papers.title: Structural basis of nucleosome recognition by the human NuA4/TIP60 acetyltransferase complex
papers.abstract: The human Tat-interactive protein, 60 kilodalton (Tip60) histone acetyltransferase (HAT) complex (NuA4/TIP60 complex, from now on TIP60-C) is a central regulator of chromatin accessibility, coupling histone acetylation with transcriptional activation and genome stability. But how the catalytic HAT module engages its nucleosome substrate has remained unknown. Here we present the structure of the human TIP60-C HAT module bound to the nucleosome, revealing a defined binding architecture in which TIP60, EPC1, ING3, and MEAF6 cooperatively position the catalytic center on the nucleosome surface, with the HAT module anchored on the histone acidic patch and engaging the linker DNA. The structure uncovers an intramolecular interaction involving the N-terminal Tudor domain of the TIP60 acetyltransferase subunit that suggests a potential mechanism for autoregulation of HAT activity. Together, our findings define the core principles by which the human TIP60-C HAT module recognizes chromatin, establishing a structural foundation for understanding how TIP60-C modifies chromatin in metazoans.

papers.title: Facilitating the identification of cryo-EM hit matter in drug discovery with Astex-Faro
papers.abstract: Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is emerging as a tool for large-scale ligand screening and fragment-based drug discovery, generating extensive collections of reconstructions. At the same time, the systematic inspection of local density variations remains challenging, particularly when identifying weak or partially occupied features. Here, we present Astex-Faro, a statistical framework that defines an expected specimen state from a reference ensemble and identifies significant structural deviations in a target map through comparison against this reference. Furthermore, the method allows the enhancement of weak or poorly resolved features, enabling the recovery of signals that would otherwise be difficult to interpret. Fourier Shell Coherence (FSCoh) is introduced as a metric that quantifies consistency across reconstruction ensembles. We show that Astex-Faro reliably detects subtle structural features and improves their interpretability across datasets spanning a broad range of experimental challenges, from highly homogeneous specimens to membrane proteins, low-occupancy ligands and fragment-screening experiments. Together, these developments provide a practical framework for cryo-EM screening, increasing confidence in hit identification and reducing the risk of missed binding events.

papers.title: STRUCTURAL PLASTICITY ALLOWS DOUBLECORTIN AND DRUG-STABILIZED MICROTUBULES TO ACCOMMODATE EACH OTHER
papers.abstract: Microtubule architecture and dynamics are modulated by small molecules, but how these compounds alter lattice properties and interactions with cellular regulators remains incompletely understood. We used the neuronal microtubule-associated protein doublecortin (DCX), previously reported to preferentially recognize 13-protofilament microtubules, to probe lattices stabilized by different taxanes, including the fluorescent taxane Fchitax-3. We show that DCX binds 15-protofilament Fchitax-3-stabilized microtubules, demonstrating that DCX is not a specific marker of 13-protofilament architecture. Cryo-electron microscopy revealed that the fluorescent moiety of Fchitax-3 inserts into inter-protofilament lateral contacts, explaining its effects on microtubule architecture and dynamics. DCX binds Fchitax-3 microtubules through its N-terminal DC domain, which accommodates the narrower inter-protofilament binding site in the 15-protofilament lattice. Remarkably, although Fchitax-3 induces the longitudinal lattice expansion characteristic of taxanes, DCX remodels its binding site towards its preferred compacted configuration. Thus, taxanes can modify microtubule structure in distinct ways while preserving lattice plasticity and the capacity to undergo conformational remodelling by microtubule-associated proteins. This contrasts with the comparatively rigid lattice of GMPCPP-stabilized microtubules. Consequently, interpretations of microtubule lattice states based on comparisons between taxane- and GMPCPP-stabilized microtubules may conflate structural differences with different degrees of lattice plasticity. Our findings establish the microtubule lattice as a malleable structural substrate whose drug-induced conformations can be further remodelled by cellular binding partners.

papers.title: A topoietic model of collective morphogenesis and compartmentalization
papers.abstract: Xenopus laevis embryos survive teratogenic stress at significantly higher rates in larger groups, a phenomenon termed cross-embryo morphogenetic assistance (CEMA) (Tung, Sperry et al. 2024). We introduce topoiesis, a proposed mechanism by which a constitutively secreted stress signal (extracellular ATP or adenosine) diffuses and decays across the group, accumulating more in larger groups where interior volume outpaces absorbing surface. We find that this rising field carries more embryos to survival and demarcates the collective more sharply from its surroundings as collective screening strength grows with size. At intermediate sizes the outcome is spatially organized (a rescued interior enclosed by a failing periphery) and reconstitutes after shuffling. In larger groups the field restructures: its peak concentration keeps rising while its interior gradient flattens into a near-uniform bulk bounded by a sharp rim, sharpening demarcation while blurring distinctions among interior members. This pre-pattern stabilizes well before individual fate commitment, opening a window in which collective geometry can act on survival outcome. A biophysically calibrated minimal model capturing these principles recapitulates CEMA rescue rates across all six observed group sizes (N=1-306; 0%-92%) and the size-dependent craniofacial defect rate among survivors. It predicts that sealing a group's boundary against loss, rather than changing its size or biochemical regulation, moves mean rescue from 0% to 100% and reorganizes the rescue structure, tracking the predicted field geometry. These results reveal a hidden simplicity behind apparent complexity: diffusion and geometry alone may suffice to make a collective both spatially organized and controllable through macroscale intervention rather than microscale engineering of its members.

papers.title: Massively parallel quantification and prediction of monomeric protein yield in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: Obtaining sufficient quantities of purified proteins in their intended molecular states is essential for biological research and protein engineering. Advances in computational protein design have expanded the functional capabilities of de novo proteins and accelerated candidate generation. However, reliable methods for ranking expected monomeric yield of candidate de novo designs, including molecular binders, fluorescent proteins and enzymes, have yet to be established. Standardized measurements of monomeric yield across diverse sequences remain scarce, limiting our understanding of its determinants and the development of accurate predictors for candidate selection. Here we developed a scalable pooled assay combining peptide barcodes, size-exclusion chromatography and mass spectrometry to quantify monomeric yield for over 39,000 natural protein domain variants, de novo proteins and nanobodies under uniform and standardized Escherichia coli production conditions. We used this dataset to (1) quantify the relationship between folding stability and monomeric yield, (2) benchmark inverse-folding methods, (3) evaluate the utility of structure-prediction confidence metrics in selecting high-yield design candidates, and (4) identify sequence and structural patterns in nanobodies associated with monomeric yield and monomer-to-dimer yield ratios. We further developed ESMC-MonoYield, a protein language model fine-tuned to predict monomeric yield from amino acid sequence alone, and prospectively demonstrated enrichment of high-yield candidates among BindCraft-designed binders. Our approach enables standardized, large-scale measurement of monomeric yield across diverse proteins, and establishes monomeric yield as a sequence-encoded property that can be learned, predicted and ultimately designed.

papers.title: A Phenomenological Model of Synaptic Activity in the Blowfly Lamina
papers.abstract: Estimates of the effective Poisson rate obtained from voltage recordings of Large Monopolar Cells (LMCs) in the blowfly lamina, measured in response to repeated light-contrast stimuli, are on the order of 5x105 events per second. These values imply that if vesicle exocytosis at photoreceptor-LMC synapse consisted of statistically independent quantal release events, the mean release rate would need to be at least this large to account for the observed signal and noise characteristics. Such a scenario is highly implausible, as it would correspond to an exocytosis rate of approximately 400 vesicles per second per active zone, or equivalently to the turnover of a membrane area comparable to that of all six photoreceptor axon terminals within a lamina cartridge more than twice per second. Relaxing the assumption of statistical independence, however, allows for substantially larger effective Poisson rates. In earlier work, we demonstrated that temporal regularization of release events- particularly through a reduction in low-frequency noise power spectral density- can increase the effective Poisson rate without altering the underlying mean release rate. Additionally, the contrast-to-current impulse response function of the extracellular space has been shown to be approximately equal in magnitude and opposite in sign to that of the LMCs, suggesting that both signals arise from the same chloride current. This observation provides a potential physiological mechanism for vesicle regularization, although it was previously described only in qualitative and simplified terms. In the present work, we develop a phenomenological model that incorporates these findings together with additional physiological parameters from literature to account for the regularization of vesicle release.

papers.title: The Molecular Interplay of Tau and Motor Proteins on Microtubules
papers.abstract: Tau is a microtubule (MT)-associated protein essential for neuronal cytoskeletal organization and intracellular transport, yet how tau physically regulates motor proteins remains elusive. Here, we integrate single-molecule imaging, cryo-electron microscopy, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying tau-mediated inhibition of kinesin-1 and cytoplasmic dynein motility. We show that tau suppresses MT landing and triggers frequent pausing and premature detachment when motors encounter tau-enriched patches. Unexpectedly, tau impairs each motor using different mechanisms. Tau and kinesin-1 compete for the same surface on tubulin, precluding simultaneous binding to the same MT site. On the other hand, while dynein and tau can co-occupy the same tubulin, tau inhibits the transition of dynein into its high-affinity MT-binding state. Thus, tau can act as a physical or a conformational roadblock in a concentration-dependent manner, exerting distinct structural constraints on kinesin and dynein transport. These findings establish a structural framework for tau-mediated regulation of axonal transport.

papers.title: Relaxation kinetics controls cell transport in crowded active monolayers
papers.abstract: Soft cancer cells embedded in stiffer epithelial layers migrate in bursts, which prior simulations have attributed to their deformability. In a dense layer, however, interfacial tension sets two things at once: the energy cost of a deformation and the rate at which it relaxes. Here we disentangle the two in an active phase-field model of a near-confluent monolayer in which relaxation rate and free energy can be varied independently. Crowding slows cells not by pushing them back bodily but through the relaxation of their own deformations against neighbours, which cancels most of their propulsion. Slowing this relaxation in a minority of cells, at unchanged energetics and propulsion, more than doubles their transport and speeds up the untouched majority by half. Conversely, the advantage of soft cells vanishes, and at high soft-cell fractions reverses, once their relaxation is made as fast as that of normal cells. Independent of composition, mixtures transport like a uniform layer with the geometric-mean interfacial tension. Passive relaxation kinetics thus emerges as an independent lever on transport, suggesting that the fluidity of heterogeneous tissues may depend on how quickly cells recover their shape, not only on how stiff they are.

papers.title: Functional Screening of Kv7.5 Channel Variants Associated with Neuronal Dysfunction
papers.abstract: The KCNQ5 gene encodes Kv7.5 channels, which contribute to the regulation of neuronal excitability. Kv7.5 genetic variants associated with neurological dysfunction have been reported, but functional characterization of Kv7.5 variants is limited and causal links to pathogenicity are lacking. We have conducted the first automated patch clamp functional screen of a panel of heterozygous Kv7.5/Kv7.3 channel variants. We tested nine mutations located in diverse locations throughout the Kv7.5 channel and identified some variants with gain-of-function effects (L341I+/-, G347S+/-, P369R+/-, R497C+/-), some with loss-of-function effects (V145G+/-, W303C+/-), and others with no apparent effect (A131V+/-, R359H+/-, R491H+/-). Variants produced a gain of function by left-shifting the voltage-dependence of channel activation alone or in combination with increasing current density. Loss of function occurred as a result of reduced current density. Using these findings, we initiated the first z-score classification to guide understanding of Kv7.5 variant pathogenicity, which can be refined as more variants are functionally characterized and new variants are discovered. Lastly, we observed higher sensitivity to channel block by XE991 in L341I+/-, G347S+/-, P369R+/- gain-of-function variants indicating potential for targeted pharmacogenetic approaches to restore normal Kv7.5 channel function.

papers.title: Scalable Contact-Gated Stochastic Operators and Universal Reduction Laws for Macromolecular Protein Dynamics, Allostery, and Kinetics
papers.abstract: Constructing continuous, thermodynamically reversible reduced equations of motion from atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) that scale from fast-folding miniproteins to multi-domain allosteric enzymes in explicit water remains a foundational problem in computational biophysics. Across 15 molecular systems (890,000 SHA-256-verified frames, 0.89 us cumulative sampling) spanning 13 structurally diverse proteins from Chignolin (d=18) to explicit-solvent Adenylate Kinase (d=426, 40,110 particles) and Maltose-Binding Protein (d=738, 49,215 particles), plus two analytical verification peptides (d=2, 4), we formulate a contact-gated, GENERIC-regularized stochastic operator on the backbone torus T^d. We show that collective slow modes compress sub-linearly across two orders of magnitude in chain length - with spectral participation ratio scaling as PR(d)=1.061 d^0.494 (95% CI [0.332, 0.666], Delta AICc=-18.15) and short-time diffusion rank as r_D^90(d)=0.799 d^0.930 (Delta AICc=-14.39) - whereas cumulative 90% equilibrium variance in large native-basin enzymes transitions to extensive proportionality (10.0% blind extrapolation error vs. 35.7% for small-protein power laws). Consequently, macromolecular tractability above d>200 requires off-diagonal sparsity rather than global PCA truncation alone: universal peptide-plane crankshaft anti-correlation (mean R(psi_i, phi_i+1)=-0.603 +/- 0.054) and sparse 3D tertiary contact gating (mean k_eff=5.97, reaching 99.3% sparsity at d=738) enable a sparse directed acyclic contact-graph Cholesky estimator scaling empirically as O(d^0.92) in time and O(d^1.06) in memory (65.8x memory compression, 99.6x faster than Graphical LASSO, and higher blind held-out log-likelihood +0.303/d vs. dense +0.205/d on MBP). Biophysically, relative solvent-accessible surface area (rSASA_i) unifies dry linear equipartition in protein cores (alpha_core=1.00, 12.33% blind thermal error) with viscosity-coupled loops (alpha_loop=1.28) and peptides (alpha_peptide=1.57); parameter-free kinematic projection reproduces solution NMR Lipari-Szabo S^2 order parameters (mean r_s=+0.483 across four BMRB enzymes, Ubiquitin Pearson r=+0.921) and X-ray B-factors (mean r_s=+0.276); and 13-fold zero-shot Leave-One-Protein-Out transfer predicts unseen protein operators directly from static PDB coordinates (r_s=+0.706, R^2=+0.359 ridge; r_s=+0.721, R^2=+0.410 GBDT). Applied to functional discovery, explicit-solvent apo toroidal operators localize mechanical domain-closure hinges in AdK (PR-AUC=0.348) and MBP (AUROC=0.690 vs. 0.446 ANM), resolve distal Met20 FG catalytic loop coupling in E. coli DHFR (71.6% recovery at 93.2% sparsity) and beta1-beta2 Ile44 routing in Ubiquitin (7.1x amplification) on blind trajectories, and quantify sub-diffusive Mori-Zwanzig reaction-coordinate memory (mean gamma_M=0.593 +/- 0.126). A validation-tuned head-to-head benchmark against Markov State Models, TICA, Smoluchowski diffusion, Elastic Network Models, and unconstrained SDEs across all 13 proteins maps the physical regimes where continuous contact-gated GENERIC operators (lowest Frobenius error 0.288, exact 0.000 spurious entropy vs. median 65.79 kB/ns/d, IQR 53.76-104.66, mean 346.17) and discrete or harmonic baselines each excel.

papers.title: Molecular machines measure the nanomechanics of biological membranes
papers.abstract: Mechanical properties such as elastic resistance to distortion define many materials and can routinely be measured with an indenting tip as simple as a finger. We have miniaturized the indentation principle by 8 orders of magnitude to analyze lipid bilayer nanomechanics, which are of relevance in biology and disease progression. Our nanoscale indenting tip is designed with DNA nanotechnology to be an integral part of a molecular machine which autonomously binds to membranes, actively indents localized membrane patches, measures the membranes elastic response to indentation, and converts the indentation degree into an optical readout signal. Compared to serially operated macro-to-microscale indentation probes, our miniaturization strategy enables deploying millions of the indenting machines for parallel analysis of membrane elasticity. The nanoscale molecular machines are also taken up by biological cells to reveal softer inner membrane compartments compared to stiffer cytoplasmic membranes, using indentation depths of solely up to 1 nm. We envision the DNA-based nanotools to contribute to the analysis of membrane mechanics of cells as well as soft polymeric interphases.

papers.title: Influence of antibody-antigen interaction on fluorescence of Rhodamine 6G conjugated to the antibodies measured in human serum
papers.abstract: Fluorescent dyes conjugated to monoclonal antibodies specifically trastuzumab (TRAS) and pertuzumab (PERT) serve as sensitive reporters of changes in the local energetic environment arising from antibody-antibody and antibody-antigen interactions. Upon covalent conjugation, the antibody local environment perturbates the energetic state of the dye, resulting in changes of the fluorescence emission energy and emission width of the dye. The dependence of these spectral parameters on antibody concentration was measured in HBS-8, diluted and undiluted human serum. In addition, the emission energy and emission width of dye-conjugated TRAS were investigated as a function of recombinant human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) extracellular domain concentration in HBS-8 and in diluted and undiluted human serum. Antibody-antibody and antibody-antigen interactions produce remarkable contributions into the emission energy and emission width. These contributions depend on the composition of the surrounding medium. Our study showed that the samples containing 100 nM TRAS in serum exhibited the largest spectral changes upon interaction with HER2 suggesting that antibody-antigen interaction are not linear across concentration range of the antibodies. Moreover, our results demonstrate that interactions between dye-conjugated antibodies and their binding partners can be detected under physiologically relevant conditions. These findings establish fluorescence emission energy and emission width analysis as a potential approach for probing antibody interactions in complex biological matrices.

papers.title: FoxO1 and HNF1α cooperatively remodel nucleosome architecture and mechanical stability to activate transcription
papers.abstract: How different transcription factors (TFs) cooperate to bind nucleosomal DNA targets remains unclear. Cryo-EM and force spectroscopy show that the pioneer factor FoxO1 binds superhelical location (SHL) +2 of nucleosomes assembled on the human IGFBP1 promoter, enhances distal DNA unwrapping, destabilizes the histone core, and reduces nucleosome mechanical stability. TF HNF1 binds SHL +5/+7 as a dimer, induces extensive DNA unwrapping without perturbing the histone core, and reshapes nucleosome disassembly dynamics. FoxO1 enhances HNF1 recruitment, and together they stabilize the nucleosome during its mechanically-induced disassembly trajectories. In-cell nucleosome footprinting on active promoters shows that FoxO1 binding enhances unwrapped nucleosomes and subnucleosomes presence, while HNF1 increases stabilized and breathing nucleosomes and reduces the subnucleosome population. Combined, they display an intermediate nucleosome phenotype. Our data leads to a model where FoxO1 destabilizes the nucleosome and enhances HNF1 recruitment, and together they remodel nucleosome architecture both in vitro and in native chromatin.

papers.title: Particle picking and centering in cryo-electron micrographs via a vanishing radial kernel
papers.abstract: A training-free procedure combines particle picking and approximate centering in cryo-electron microscopy through a single convolution of the micrograph with a compact radial kernel, whose weights increase with distance from the origin, saturate in an annulus, and vanish beyond it. Particles are darker than their surroundings and much weaker than the noise; each carves a well in the response, and local minima of the response are candidate centers. Constant background offsets leave these extrema unchanged away from image boundaries, and a local stability bound controls the displacement of a well's minimum under signed perturbations without assuming a symmetric particle. Grid seeds are iteratively updated, nearby endpoints are merged, and two-dimensional classification follows. On the emph{Plasmodium falciparum} 80S ribosome and $beta$-galactosidase data sets, reconstructions reach 3.68 and 4.30~AA{}, compared with 3.77 and 4.36~AA{} using reference coordinates, with picking at 0.20--0.26~s per micrograph.

papers.title: Learning inhibitor interactions from protein deep mutational scanning data and deep learning models
papers.abstract: Recent advances in protein language models, geometric deep learning, and structure prediction frameworks have the potential to accelerate computational drug discovery. However, it remains unclear how well these methods generalize beyond their training sets. Mutation-dependent drug responses present a challenge to these methods because there are often large effects from relatively small perturbations. Here, we systematically benchmark diverse mutational effect and drug-target affinity prediction models using deep mutational scanning datasets spanning 11 inhibitor conditions for the MET kinase domain. Across both mutational effect prediction and drug-target affinity tasks, current AI models produce largely ligand-invariant predictions despite experimentally distinct inhibitor-dependent fitness landscapes. Ligand-aware geometric models, including LigandMPNN and LASErMPNN, partially recover experimentally validated resistance-associated hotspots, highlighting the importance of explicitly modeling protein-ligand interactions and local structural flexibility. In contrast, deep learning affinity prediction models underestimate mutation-induced changes in binding affinity. This deficiency likely reflects mutation-invariant structural priors derived from co-folded structure prediction frameworks and the absence of mutation-conditioned supervision in current affinity datasets. Finally, we further extended our analysis to several kinase-inhibitor deep mutational scanning datasets and confirm the overall trends. Our findings suggest that a primary limitation in improving performance on this task lies in the scarcity of mutation-conditioned protein-ligand training data rather than model architecture alone.

papers.title: Comparative cryo-EM structures of CGMMV and ToMMV reveal divergent coat protein packing and electrostatics indicating Tobamovirus host specificity
papers.abstract: Tobamoviruses are a group of economically important plant viruses exhibiting extreme stability and persistence. Despite high morphological similarity, they show extensive host-family specificity, cause a range of symptoms, and cause significant global yield loss in fruit and vegetable plants. Composed of a rod-shaped helical assembly of identical coat proteins encasing a single-stranded RNA, Tobamoviruses have long served as fundamental models for understanding helical assemblies. Here we report the cryo-EM structures of two viruses from this genus, CGMMV and ToMMV, at 2.86 [A] and 2.71 [A] resolution, respectively. The structures reveal divergent packing strategies within the virion assembly. While ToMMV is genetically similar to the canonical Tobamovirus TMV and displays a structure closely resembling TMV, CGMMV employs a more hydrophobic packing strategy, particularly in the solvent-exposed inner loop region of the coat protein. Comparative biophysical and molecular dynamics analyses from the reconstructed structures reveal more stable and compact protein packing for CGMMV at both the subunit and assembly levels. Furthermore, this study reports a newly identified electrostatic patch existing at the lower alpha-helix region of the coat protein that serves as an additional RNA-stabilizing region, with host family-specific amino acid substitutions among Tobamoviruses. Our study elucidates the structural mechanics and evolutionary strategies driving virion stability and host diversity while maintaining a conserved helical assembly. These findings reveal how subtle electrostatic tuning and divergent packing strategies drive viral stability and host adaptation within a strictly conserved quaternary scaffold.

papers.title: Bottom-heaviness stabilizes pelagic fish eggs and generates advective transport at their surface
papers.abstract: Pelagic fish eggs are small spheres (~1 mm) that drift in the open ocean, carried by large-scale currents. Embedded in these currents are egg-scale turbulent eddies that impose local rotational forcing on the eggs. Accordingly, eggs are considered passive tracer particles that move with these eddies, implying that mass transfer of oxygen and waste are controlled only by molecular diffusion. However, eggs are bottom heavy, characterized by a dense embryo and a buoyant oil globule at opposing poles. We hypothesized that such internal structure generates a gravitational restoring torque, stabilizing the egg and generating relative egg-water motion. To test this hypothesis we exposed fish eggs to controlled flows with shear levels typical of upper mixed-layer and estuarine environments, and analyzed their dynamics. Eggs displayed one of two repeatable behaviors: (i) steady orientation, with a near-constant egg angle, and (ii) revolving motion, with egg rotation at time-varying angular speed. Both behaviors generated relative motion between the eggs and the surrounding water. A rigid-body rotational model balancing external flow-induced torque and gravitational restoring torque showed that transitions between these states depend on local flow fields and developmental stage, with older eggs shifting to revolving behavior at lower external fluid torque. Together, these findings suggest that advective transport is important and that diffusion-only models underestimate exchange rates, which are a major component in predicting the effects of environmental factors on embryo survival.

papers.title: End-to-end reconstruction for cryo electron ptychographic single-particle analysis
papers.abstract: Cryo-electron ptychographic (cryo-ptycho) single-particle analysis (SPA) is a diffractive imaging method for protein structure determination. Current reconstruction workflows sequentially reconstruct a 2D phase micrograph from each scan, and then apply conventional SPA software to the resulting projections to obtain a 3D potential map. Here, we introduce End2EndPtychoSPA, an end-to-end reconstruction algorithm that directly fits a 3D electrostatic potential volume and particle poses to 4D-STEM diffraction data using a differentiable multislice forward model. On simulated haemoglobin data where the sequential route recovers initial poses, End2EndPtychoSPA with a learnable vitreous-ice layer reaches 3.22 A resolution against the ground truth (FSC 0.5), compared with 3.41 A for the sequential route. We also compare End2EndPtychoSPA with the sequential route on four published experimental cryo-ptycho SPA datasets. On apoferritin (11,552 particles), the End2EndPtychoSPA map improves agreement with an external atomic model over both our matched sequential route on the same particles and the deposited EMD-19425 half-map mean, and shifts the unmasked half-map FSC 0.143 crossing from 6.83 A to 5.99 A. On T20S, TMV and Phi92, End2EndPtychoSPA does not yet improve upon the 2D route.
